questions.q: **Directions (Q.1-6):** Read the passage carefully and answer the questions. Which of the following best describes the central theme of the passage?
options: The decline of cash transactions in large retail chains
How phone-based digital payments have transformed small Indian merchants and the challenges that remain
Why elderly customers refuse to use smartphones for shopping
The role of banks in funding grocery stores across India
questions.solution: The passage traces how QR-code based payments reached small merchants, the benefits (instant credit, loan access) and the remaining problems (uneven adoption, outages, privacy). Other options name only side details. **Answer: How phone-based digital payments have transformed small Indian merchants and the challenges that remain**
questions.passage: **Directions (Q.1-6):** Read the passage carefully and answer the questions. Walk into any small neighbourhood grocery store in India today, and you will likely see a laminated QR code taped beside the cash box. A customer finishes her shopping, points her phone camera at the code, types an amount, and within seconds the shopkeeper's phone announces the payment aloud. This small ritual, repeated millions of times a day, represents one of the fastest adoption curves of any technology in the country's history. Five years ago, digital payments in India were largely the preserve of online shopping and card swipes at larger retail chains. Small merchants either dealt only in cash or accepted cards reluctantly, since hardware terminals were costly and settlement was slow. The arrival of interoperable, phone-based transfer systems changed the calculus entirely: a merchant now needs no terminal, pays no installation fee, and receives money instantly. For a family-run store operating on thin margins, the difference is not cosmetic - it affects how much working capital stays trapped in loose change, how safely the day's earnings can be stored, and whether a customer who arrives without cash can be served at all. Economists have noted a second-order effect as well. When every sale is recorded digitally, a shop's turnover becomes visible to banks, and this visibility makes it easier for the owner to obtain small working-capital loans that were previously out of reach, because lenders had no way to judge repayment capacity. At the same time, the transition is uneven. Elderly customers and merchants in smaller towns sometimes struggle with interfaces designed for confident smartphone users; network outages can bring a counter to a halt; and the spoken announcement of every payment, while practical, has made some users uneasy about privacy. Policymakers therefore face a familiar challenge: a technology whose benefits are large but whose gains depend on the patience of first-time users. If the next phase of adoption is handled with the same simplicity that produced the first, the humble grocery counter may yet become the quiet engine of India's digital economy.

questions.q: According to the passage, why did small merchants earlier hesitate to accept card payments?
options: Because customers always preferred to pay in cash
Because the government taxed card transactions heavily
Because hardware terminals were costly and settlement of money was slow
Because banks refused to open merchant accounts for small shops
questions.solution: The passage states merchants accepted cards 'reluctantly, since hardware terminals were costly and settlement was slow'. **Answer: Because hardware terminals were costly and settlement of money was slow**

questions.q: What does the phrase 'second-order effect' mentioned in the passage refer to?
options: A fall in the price of card-swiping machines
Digital sales records making lenders willing to extend small loans to shop owners
An increase in the number of customers visiting the stores
Network outages that bring payment counters to a halt
questions.solution: 'Second-order effect' introduces the loan-access point: digital records make turnover visible to banks, so owners can obtain working-capital loans they could not get before. **Answer: Digital sales records making lenders willing to extend small loans to shop owners**

questions.q: The word 'calculus' as used in the passage most nearly means:
options: an official settlement of tax accounts
a careful weighing of costs and benefits
a fixed rule laid down by regulators
questions.solution: 'Changed the calculus entirely' refers to the merchant's mental cost-benefit calculation (terminal cost, fees, speed of money), not the subject mathematics. **Answer: a careful weighing of costs and benefits**

questions.q: The word 'uneven' as used in the passage means:
options: higher than in the previous year
not uniform across regions and groups of users
questions.solution: The next sentence explains: elderly users and small-town merchants struggle more, so adoption is 'uneven', i.e. not uniform. **Answer: not uniform across regions and groups of users**

questions.q: The author's attitude towards the spread of digital payments can best be described as:
questions.solution: The author lists real benefits but closes with warnings about first-time users and a conditional 'may yet become', i.e. hopeful but careful - cautious optimism. **Answer: cautiously optimistic**

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (1).
questions.solution: An adjective modifying 'life tool' is needed and the tone is positive: literacy is a **fundamental** (basic, essential) tool. Redundant is opposite in sense; casual and tentative weaken the claim. **Answer: fundamental**
questions.passage: **Directions (Q.7-12):** In the following passage there are blanks, each of which has been numbered. Choose the word for each blank that fits the passage best. Financial literacy is no longer an optional skill; it is a (1) ___ life tool. Yet surveys repeatedly show that a large number of young earners cannot (2) ___ between compound and simple interest, and many fall (3) ___ to misleading investment schemes. Schools teach students how to solve equations, but rarely how to draw up a household budget or read the fine print of a loan agreement. As a result, the first salary often becomes an (4) ___ for unplanned spending rather than the start of a savings habit. Experts argue that a single semester of practical money lessons - covering budgeting, the cost of borrowing, and the difference between saving and investing - could (5) ___ a lifetime of avoidable debt. The earlier these habits are formed, the more (6) ___ the benefits.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (2).
questions.solution: The structure '___ between X and Y' requires **distinguish** (tell apart). Argue would need 'over/about'; disturb and dissolve make no sense here. **Answer: distinguish**

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (3).
questions.solution: The fixed collocation is 'fall **prey** to' (become a victim of). 'Fall victim to' exists but needs no article change here 'victim' cannot drop its article, and trap/hunt break the idiom. **Answer: prey**

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (4).
questions.solution: 'An ___ for unplanned spending' - the salary becomes an **excuse** (justification) for spending. Evidence and applause do not fit 'for unplanned spending'; obstacle is opposite. **Answer: excuse**

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (5).
questions.solution: Lessons would stop ('prevent') a lifetime of avoidable debt. Prolong and postpone would extend it, and pardon is for offences. **Answer: prevent**

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (6).
questions.solution: 'The more ___ the benefits' needs an adjective meaning long-lasting: **enduring**. Endurable means bearable; ensuring and insured are wrong forms here. **Answer: enduring**

questions.q: Which of the following should be the first sentence after rearrangement?
questions.solution: The narrative opens with the founding moment in 1998 - **C**. It alone introduces Ramesh and the stall; every other sentence refers back to it. Order: C-A-D-B-E. **Answer: (C)**
questions.passage: **Directions (Q.13-17):** Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) in the proper sequence to form a meaningful paragraph and answer the questions. (A) At first, the shop sold only tea and biscuits to bus passengers who stopped there for a few minutes. (B) Over the years, the little stall grew into a two-storey eatery that now serves hundreds of travellers every day. (C) When Ramesh set up his tea stall near the highway in 1998, he had barely five hundred rupees in his pocket. (D) Encouraged by this steady demand, he slowly added snacks, and later full meals, to his menu. (E) Today his two sons manage the business, and the family often recalls how it all began with a single kettle.

questions.q: Which of the following should be the second sentence after rearrangement?
questions.solution: After the founding comes the beginning of trade: 'At first, the shop sold only tea...' - **A** follows C chronologically. Order: C-A-D-B-E. **Answer: (A)**

questions.q: Which of the following should be the third sentence after rearrangement?
questions.solution: 'Encouraged by this steady demand' needs the demand established in A (tea and biscuits selling), so **D** comes next. Order: C-A-D-B-E. **Answer: (D)**

questions.q: Which of the following should be the fourth sentence after rearrangement?
questions.solution: Growth 'over the years' into a two-storey eatery follows the menu expansion of D - **B**. Order: C-A-D-B-E. **Answer: (B)**

questions.q: Which of the following should be the fifth/last sentence after rearrangement?
questions.solution: 'Today his two sons manage...' closes the time line from 1998 to the present - **E** ends the paragraph. Order: C-A-D-B-E. **Answer: (E)**

questions.q: Read the sentence to find out whether there is any error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. The manager along with his assistants (A)/ were present at the warehouse (B)/ when the consignment arrived yesterday. (C)/ No error (D)
questions.solution: 'Along with' does not change the number of the subject; the verb must agree with 'the manager' (singular): **was present**. **Answer: B**

questions.q: Read the sentence to find out whether there is any error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. One of my friends who is (A)/ a chartered accountant by profession (B)/ have agreed to audit our accounts. (C)/ No error (D)
questions.solution: The subject is 'One' (of my friends), which is singular, so the verb must be **has agreed**, not 'have agreed'. **Answer: C**

questions.q: Read the sentence to find out whether there is any error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. She has been working (A)/ in this organisation since (B)/ more than ten years. (C)/ No error (D)
questions.solution: 'Since' is used with a point of time; with a period ('more than ten years') the correct preposition is **for**. **Answer: C**

questions.q: Read the sentence to find out whether there is any error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. The numbers of applicants (A)/ for the clerical examination (B)/ has risen sharply this year. (C)/ No error (D)
questions.solution: 'The number of' (singular, meaning the count) is the correct subject phrase; 'The numbers of' is unidiomatic here. Error is in **A**. **Answer: A**

questions.q: Read the sentence to find out whether there is any error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Neither the supervisor nor (A)/ the workers was willing (B)/ to stay back after office hours. (C)/ No error (D)
questions.solution: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'the workers' (plural): **were willing**. **Answer: B**

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
questions.solution: 'Decided to' takes the base form of the verb: decided to **hike** (raise). 'Hiked/hiking' break the infinitive and 'hasty' is an adjective. **Answer: hike**

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
questions.solution: The phrasal verb 'call off' means to cancel or stop an event. 'Called out/over/of' do not convey cancellation. **Answer: off**

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
questions.solution: The clause 'never lends money' demands the negative quality of being **miserly** (stingy). Generous, lavish and charitable all mean the opposite. **Answer: miserly**

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
questions.solution: Passive voice ('were ___ by') needs the past participle: were **accepted**. Accepting/accept are active forms and 'acceptance' is a noun. **Answer: accepted**

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
questions.solution: 'Hardly had... when' is the fixed correlative pair; 'no sooner' pairs with 'than', not 'hardly'. **Answer: when**

questions.q: In which of the following senses is the bold word used in the given sentence? Choose the option closest in meaning to the word **as used in the sentence**: **settle**: 'The company finally decided to settle the dispute out of court.'
questions.solution: Here 'settle' means to bring a dispute to an end, so its closest meaning is **resolve**. Sink, lodge and decorate suit other senses (sink down, lodge a complaint) but not this one. **Answer: resolve**

questions.q: In which of the following senses is the bold word used in the given sentence? Choose the option closest in meaning to the word **as used in the sentence**: **draw**: 'The teacher asked the students to draw a map of their neighbourhood.'
questions.solution: 'Draw a map' = make a line picture, i.e. **sketch**. Attract, pull and end fit 'draw' in other collocations (draw a crowd, draw a cart, draw to an end). **Answer: sketch**

questions.q: In which of the following senses is the bold word used in the given sentence? Choose the option closest in meaning to the word **as used in the sentence**: **paper**: 'The minister tried to paper over the differences between the two alliance partners.'
questions.solution: The idiom 'paper over' means to hide or gloss over problems: **conceal**. The literal senses wrap, publish, fold are not meant here. **Answer: conceal**
